question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

The corridor was completely empty (a)/ because the school bell (b)/ had already rang for the assembly. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (c).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The verb "ring" has the forms ring – rang – rung. After the auxiliary "had" (past perfect), the third form (V3) must be used. So "had already rang" must be "had already rung".

◦ Corrected sentence: The corridor was completely empty because the school bell had already rung for the assembly.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The corridor was completely empty" is a proper simple past clause, and "completely" is correctly used as an adverb before the adjective "empty".

 

• Part (b) is correct — "because the school bell" is a proper conjunction followed by a singular subject.

 

• Option (d) No error — cannot be selected, because "had already rang" in part (c) is incorrect.

 

NOTE

 

• ring – rang – rung, sing – sang – sung, drink – drank – drunk, sink – sank – sunk: V2 and V3 are different in these verbs, so never use had rang, has drank, have sank (perfect tenses need V3).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

The priceless jewels were stole (a)/ from the museum last night, (b)/ according to the police report. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. (a).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The passive voice is formed with "be + third form (V3)". The verb "steal" has the forms steal – stole – stolen, so "were stole" must be "were stolen".

◦ Corrected sentence: The priceless jewels were stolen from the museum last night, according to the police report.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (b) is correct — "from the museum last night," is a proper prepositional phrase of place followed by an adverb of past time.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "according to the police report." is a proper prepositional phrase that gives the source of the information.

 

• Option (d) No error — cannot be selected, because "were stole" in part (a) is incorrect.

 

NOTE

 

• steal – stole – stolen, break – broke – broken, choose – chose – chosen, speak – spoke – spoken, write – wrote – written: the passive and the perfect tenses need V3 — was stolen, has been broken, is spoken.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

Last month, (a)/ the workers lay the foundation (b)/ of the new district hospital. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (b).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Lay" (= to put or place) is a transitive verb with the forms lay – laid – laid, and it needs an object. Here the object is "the foundation" and the time is past ("Last month"), so "lay" must be "laid".

◦ Corrected sentence: Last month, the workers laid the foundation of the new district hospital.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "Last month," is a proper introductory adverbial phrase of past time.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "of the new district hospital." is a proper prepositional phrase that completes the noun "foundation".

 

• Option (d) No error — cannot be selected, because "lay" in part (b) is the wrong form.

 

NOTE

 

• lay – laid – laid (to put; takes an object): lay the table, lay an egg, lay a foundation; lie – lay – lain (to rest; no object): lie on the bed; lie – lied – lied (to tell an untruth).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

The discussions had not yet began (a)/ although all the delegates (b)/ had reached the venue in the morning. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. (a).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The verb "begin" has the forms begin – began – begun. After "had" (past perfect), the third form (V3) must be used, so "had not yet began" must be "had not yet begun".

◦ Corrected sentence: The discussions had not yet begun although all the delegates had reached the venue in the morning.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (b) is correct — "although all the delegates" is a proper conjunction followed by a plural subject.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "had reached the venue in the morning." is a proper past perfect verb phrase, and "reach" takes its object directly.

 

• Option (d) No error — cannot be selected, because "had not yet began" in part (a) is incorrect.

 

NOTE

 

• begin – began – begun, run – ran – run, come – came – come, become – became – become: never use V2 after has / have / had — has began, had ran are wrong.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

During the heavy flood, (a)/ the old bridge was collapsed (b)/ and cut off several villages. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (b).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Collapse" is an intransitive verb, which means it does not take an object. Only transitive verbs can be used in the passive voice, so "was collapsed" must be "collapsed".

◦ Corrected sentence: During the heavy flood, the old bridge collapsed and cut off several villages.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "During the heavy flood," is a proper prepositional phrase of time.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "and cut off several villages." is a proper coordinate verb phrase, and "cut off" (past form the same as the present form) matches the past tense.

 

• Option (d) No error — cannot be selected, because "was collapsed" in part (b) is incorrect.

 

NOTE

 

• Intransitive verbs have no passive voice: collapse, happen, occur, arrive, die, fall, appear, vanish, exist — never was collapsed, was happened, was occurred.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

The retired soldier (a)/ found the missing child (b)/ laying unconscious under a tree. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (c).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Lie" (= to be in a resting position) is an intransitive verb with the forms lie – lay – lain – lying. "Laying" is the -ing form of "lay" (= to put), which needs an object. The child is resting, not putting anything, so "laying" must be "lying".

◦ Corrected sentence: The retired soldier found the missing child lying unconscious under a tree.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The retired soldier" is a proper singular subject with the participial adjective "retired".

 

• Part (b) is correct — "found the missing child" is a proper simple past verb phrase with an object.

 

• Option (d) No error — cannot be selected, because "laying" in part (c) is incorrect.

 

NOTE

 

• The book is lying on the table (rest, no object) but She is laying the table (put, with object); He is lying (telling an untruth) — three different verbs are involved: lie / lay / lie.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

The engineers who were designed (a)/ the new metro station (b)/ received an award from the government. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. (a).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The relative clause has an object ("the new metro station"), so its verb must be transitive and active. "Were designed" is passive and cannot be followed by an object. So "who were designed" must be "who designed".

◦ Corrected sentence: The engineers who designed the new metro station received an award from the government.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (b) is correct — "the new metro station" is a proper object noun phrase.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "received an award from the government." is a proper simple past main verb phrase that agrees with the plural subject "engineers".

 

• Option (d) No error — cannot be selected, because "were designed" in part (a) is incorrect.

 

NOTE

 

• Active: The engineers who designed the station received an award; passive: The station, which was designed by the engineers, won an award. A passive verb is never followed by an object.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

Historians regard (a)/ Ashoka one of the greatest (b)/ rulers of ancient India. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (b).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The verb "regard" is followed by object + "as" + complement: "regard X as Y". So "regard Ashoka one of the greatest" must be "regard Ashoka as one of the greatest".

◦ Corrected sentence: Historians regard Ashoka as one of the greatest rulers of ancient India.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "Historians regard" is a proper plural subject with a simple present verb for a general statement.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "rulers of ancient India." is a proper noun phrase, and the plural "rulers" correctly follows "one of the greatest".

 

• Option (d) No error — cannot be selected, because "as" is missing in part (b).

 

NOTE

 

• regard X as Y, look upon X as Y, think of X as Y, treat X as Y, describe X as Y (with "as") but consider X Y, deem X Y, call X Y (without "as").

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

It has been a long time, (a)/ so I am really looking forward (b)/ to meet you at the reunion. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (c).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In the phrase "look forward to", the word "to" is a preposition, and a preposition is followed by a noun or a gerund (-ing form). So "to meet" must be "to meeting".

◦ Corrected sentence: It has been a long time, so I am really looking forward to meeting you at the reunion.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "It has been a long time," is a proper present perfect clause for a period that continues up to now.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "so I am really looking forward" is a proper present continuous verb phrase, and "really" correctly modifies the verb.

 

• Option (d) No error — cannot be selected, because "to meet" in part (c) is incorrect.

 

NOTE

 

• Preposition "to" + gerund: look forward to meeting, object to paying, be used to waking, in addition to teaching; infinitive "to" + base verb: I want to meet you, He hopes to win.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

The organising committee suggested to postpone (a)/ the annual function (b)/ because of the heavy floods. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. (a).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The verb "suggest" is followed by a gerund (-ing form), or by a "that"-clause, and never by a to-infinitive. So "suggested to postpone" must be "suggested postponing".

◦ Corrected sentence: The organising committee suggested postponing the annual function because of the heavy floods.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (b) is correct — "the annual function" is a proper object noun phrase.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "because of the heavy floods." is a proper prepositional phrase of reason.

 

• Option (d) No error — cannot be selected, because "suggested to postpone" in part (a) is incorrect.

 

NOTE

 

• Verbs followed by a gerund: suggest, avoid, enjoy, mind, deny, finish, postpone, admit, practise, consider — She suggested going, He avoided meeting; or suggested that we should go.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

Over thousands of years, (a)/ polar bears have adopted themselves (b)/ to the extreme Arctic cold. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (b).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Adapt" means to adjust oneself to new conditions, and it is used with "to". "Adopt" means to take up or accept something as one's own (a child, a plan, a habit). The sense here is adjusting to the cold, so "adopted" must be "adapted".

◦ Corrected sentence: Over thousands of years, polar bears have adapted themselves to the extreme Arctic cold.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "Over thousands of years," is a proper introductory prepositional phrase of duration.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "to the extreme Arctic cold." is a proper prepositional phrase, since "adapt" takes "to".

 

• Option (d) No error — cannot be selected, because "adopted" in part (b) is the wrong word.

 

NOTE

 

• adapt (adjust) — adapt to a new climate; adopt (take up) — adopt a child, adopt a new policy; adept (skilled) — adept at chess.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

Late at night, (a)/ two masked men broke into the shop (b)/ and robbed all the jewellery. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (c).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The verb "rob" takes a person or a place as its object (rob a bank, rob a man of his wallet). The things taken are described with "steal". So "robbed all the jewellery" must be "stole all the jewellery".

◦ Corrected sentence: Late at night, two masked men broke into the shop and stole all the jewellery.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "Late at night," is a proper introductory adverbial phrase of time.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "two masked men broke into the shop" is a proper simple past clause, and "broke" is the correct past form of "break".

 

• Option (d) No error — cannot be selected, because "robbed" in part (c) is the wrong verb.

 

NOTE

 

• rob someone or somewhere (of something) — rob a bank, rob a traveller of his purse; steal something (from someone) — steal money, steal jewellery from a shop.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

Did the manager (a)/ approved the leave application (b)/ before he left the office? (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (b).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• After the auxiliary verbs do / does / did, the main verb takes its base form (V1), because the tense is already shown by the auxiliary. So "approved" must be "approve".

◦ Corrected sentence: Did the manager approve the leave application before he left the office?

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "Did the manager" is a proper question opening, with the auxiliary before the subject.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "before he left the office?" is a proper past clause, and "left" is the correct past form of "leave".

 

• Option (d) No error — cannot be selected, because "approved" in part (b) is incorrect.

 

NOTE

 

• Did he approve?, She did not go, Does he know? — after do / does / did, use the base form; never Did he approved, He did not went.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

Not until the invigilator collected (a)/ the answer sheets did the students (b)/ realise that time was up. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. (d).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The sentence is grammatically correct. When a sentence begins with "Not until …", the main clause takes inversion (the auxiliary comes before the subject), so "did the students realise" is correct. After "did", the base form "realise" is used.

◦ Sentence as given: Not until the invigilator collected the answer sheets did the students realise that time was up.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "Not until the invigilator collected" is a proper introductory clause with the simple past and the normal order of subject and verb.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "the answer sheets did the students" correctly places the auxiliary "did" before the subject "the students".

 

• Part (c) is correct — "realise that time was up." uses the correct base form after "did", followed by a proper noun clause.

 

NOTE

 

• Do not over-correct: Not until the bell rang did he leave; Never have I seen such a match; Hardly had she arrived when it began to rain — after a negative adverbial at the start, the auxiliary comes before the subject.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

My cousin (a)/ is teaching in this school (b)/ since 2015. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (b).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Since" is followed by a point of time, and the action that began then and still continues needs the present perfect (continuous) tense, and not the present continuous. So "is teaching" must be "has been teaching".

◦ Corrected sentence: My cousin has been teaching in this school since 2015.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "My cousin" is a proper singular subject.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "since 2015." is a proper use of "since" with a point of time.

 

• Option (d) No error — cannot be selected, because "is teaching" in part (b) is incorrect.

 

NOTE

 

• Since (point of time) and for (period) — He has been living here since 2010 / for ten years; never He is living here since 2010.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The auditors who examined (a)/ the accounts of the company (b)/ has finally submitted (c)/ their report to the board. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (c).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A verb must agree with its subject, which is "The auditors" (plural), and not with the nearby noun "company". So the singular "has finally submitted" must be the plural "have finally submitted".

◦ Corrected sentence: The auditors who examined the accounts of the company have finally submitted their report to the board.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The auditors who examined" is a proper plural subject with a relative clause in the simple past.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "the accounts of the company" is a proper object noun phrase.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "their report to the board." is proper, and the plural "their" agrees with "The auditors".

 

NOTE

 

• The verb agrees with the head noun of the subject: The quality of the products has fallen; The teacher, along with her students, is present; The auditors who examined the accounts have submitted.

question:
Select the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The driver could not avoid to hit the cyclist who suddenly crossed the road.
option_3: the cyclist who suddenly crossed the road
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. avoid to hit.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The verb "avoid" is followed by a gerund (-ing form), and never by a to-infinitive. So "avoid to hit" must be "avoid hitting".

◦ Corrected sentence: The driver could not avoid hitting the cyclist who suddenly crossed the road.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "could not" — this is correct, because the modal "could not" is properly followed by a base verb.

 

• Option 2: "The driver" — this is correct, because it is a proper singular subject.

 

• Option 3: "the cyclist who suddenly crossed the road" — this is correct, because it is a proper object with a relative clause in the simple past.

 

NOTE

 

• Verbs followed by a gerund: avoid hitting, enjoy reading, mind waiting, finish writing, risk losing, escape being caught. Compare: decide to go, hope to win (to-infinitive).

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

Yesterday, the guide lead the tourists through the narrow cave.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. led.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The verb "lead" has the forms lead – led – led. The adverb "Yesterday" shows past time, so the past form "led" must be used, and the sentence must read "the guide led the tourists".

◦ Corrected sentence: Yesterday, the guide led the tourists through the narrow cave.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: "leads" — this is a simple present form, which does not fit "Yesterday".

 

• Option 3: "leaded" — this is not a verb form of "lead"; "leaded" is an adjective (as in "leaded petrol").

 

• Option 4: No substitution required — incorrect, because "lead" is the present form and the sentence refers to past time.

 

NOTE

 

• lead – led – led, feed – fed – fed, bleed – bled – bled, speed – sped – sped (verbs); lead (the metal, said "led") is a noun. Also read – read – read (spelling same, pronunciation changes).

question:
Select the incorrectly used word in the given sentence.

 

The candidate did a fatal mistake during the interview and lost the job.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. did.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The verb that goes with "mistake" is "make", not "do". The correct collocation is "make a mistake", so "did" must be "made".

◦ Corrected sentence: The candidate made a fatal mistake during the interview and lost the job.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "fatal" — this is correct, because "fatal" means leading to failure or disaster and suits "mistake".

 

• Option 2: "during" — this is correct, because "during" is the proper preposition before the event "the interview".

 

• Option 3: "lost" — this is correct, because "lost" is the proper simple past form of "lose", matching the tense of the sentence.

 

NOTE

 

• make a mistake, an effort, progress, a promise, a decision; do homework, a favour, business, harm; take a shower, a break, a photograph, a risk; pay a visit, attention.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

Before leaving the office, please remember ___ all the lights and fans.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. to switch off.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Remember + to-infinitive" means remembering to do something that is yet to be done, while "remember + gerund" means recalling something already done. The lights are to be turned off before leaving, so the correct form is "to switch off".

◦ Complete sentence: Before leaving the office, please remember to switch off all the lights and fans.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "switching off" — this would mean recalling an act already done in the past, which does not suit "please remember" before leaving.

 

• Option 3: "to switching off" — this treats "to" as a preposition, which is not the pattern after "remember".

 

• Option 4: "having switched off" — this perfect gerund refers to an action that is already complete, which contradicts "Before leaving".

 

NOTE

 

• remember to lock (a task to do) vs remember locking (recall); forget to vs forget -ing; stop to (in order to) vs stop -ing (give up); try to (attempt) vs try -ing (experiment); regret to inform vs regret informing.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

The finance minister emphasised on the need for stricter cyber-security laws.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. emphasised the need.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The verb "emphasise" is transitive and takes its object directly, without a preposition. So "emphasised on the need" must be "emphasised the need".

◦ Corrected sentence: The finance minister emphasised the need for stricter cyber-security laws.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "emphasised about the need" — "about" is wrongly added after a transitive verb.

 

• Option 2: "emphasised to the need" — "to" is wrongly added after a transitive verb.

 

• Option 4: No improvement required — incorrect, because "on" is wrongly added after "emphasised".

 

NOTE

 

• Transitive verbs with no preposition: emphasise the need, stress the point, discuss the plan, mention the fact, describe the scene, resemble her mother; the noun takes a preposition — lay emphasis on, put stress on.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

Could you please make a favour for me and drop this letter at the post office?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. do me a favour.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The verb that goes with "favour" is "do", and the pattern is "do someone a favour" (or "do a favour for someone"). So "make a favour for me" must be "do me a favour".

◦ Corrected sentence: Could you please do me a favour and drop this letter at the post office?

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "make a favour to me" — "make" does not collocate with "favour".

 

• Option 2: "give me a favour" — "give" does not collocate with "favour"; the verb needed is "do".

 

• Option 3: "do a favour with me" — the verb "do" is right, but "with me" is the wrong pattern; it should be "do me a favour" or "do a favour for me".

 

NOTE

 

• do a favour, harm, business, homework, one's duty; make a mistake, a promise, a decision, an effort; pay a visit, attention, a compliment; give a speech, advice; take a break, a chance.

question:
Select the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The detective asked the witness how did the burglar enter the house.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. how did the burglar enter.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In an indirect (reported) question, the word order is that of a statement: subject before verb, with no auxiliary "do/does/did". So "how did the burglar enter" must be "how the burglar entered".

◦ Corrected sentence: The detective asked the witness how the burglar entered the house.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "The detective asked" — this is correct, because it is a proper singular subject with a past reporting verb.

 

• Option 2: "the witness" — this is correct, because it is a proper indirect object of "asked".

 

• Option 4: "the house" — this is correct, because "enter" is a transitive verb that takes its object without a preposition.

 

NOTE

 

• She asked where he lived (not where did he live); I wonder what he wants; direct: "Where do you live?" she asked. In indirect questions, there is no inversion and no do-support.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

If the players would have practised harder, they would have won the tournament.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. had practised.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In the third conditional (an unreal past situation), the pattern is "If + past perfect (had + V3), … would have + V3". "Would" is not used in the "if"-clause, so "would have practised" must be "had practised".

◦ Corrected sentence: If the players had practised harder, they would have won the tournament.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "have practised" — the "if"-clause needs the past perfect, not the present perfect.

 

• Option 2: "would practise" — "would" is wrongly used in the "if"-clause, and the base form does not suit an unreal past.

 

• Option 3: "having practised" — this is a participle without an auxiliary and leaves the "if"-clause without a finite verb.

 

NOTE

 

• Type 3: If he had known, he would have come; Type 2: If he knew, he would come; Type 1: If he knows, he will come. Never If + would.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

The clerk denied to have taken the money from the drawer.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. having taken.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The verb "deny" is followed by a gerund (-ing form), and not by a to-infinitive. So "denied to have taken" must be "denied having taken".

◦ Corrected sentence: The clerk denied having taken the money from the drawer.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: "for taking" — "deny" does not take the preposition "for".

 

• Option 3: "to take" — the to-infinitive is wrong after "deny".

 

• Option 4: No substitution required — incorrect, because "to have taken" is a to-infinitive, which "deny" does not take.

 

NOTE

 

• deny / admit / regret / recall + gerund: denied having taken, admitted stealing, regretted losing, recalled meeting; compare refused to pay, agreed to help (to-infinitive).
